title: These 5 Things, All Year Long
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This long overview introduces Dave Stuart Jr.'s Non-Freaked Out framework, a short list of literacy habits meant to focus a content-area teacher's year on thinking, reading, writing, speaking and becoming a better person. He presents it as a smarter-not-harder response to teacher overload that strengthens content knowledge rather than replacing it. Argument sits at the center as collaborative, virtue-building thought rather than antagonism, and he works through how reading, writing and discussion can all feed it. A classroom video of a pop-up debate on Picasso's Guernica illustrates the approach and the formative data it yields. He frames the whole thing as rough-draft thinking that teachers should adapt, and the argument is about what and how to teach, so it is Learning and Curriculum.
points: The framework limits teachers to a few instructional habits so that focus, not exhaustion, drives literacy growth across subjects.
It explicitly protects content-rich curricula; the habits are a pathway through content, not a substitute for it.
Argument is defined as seeking a good decision with fairness and humility, not victory, which makes it a vehicle for character as well as thinking.
Listening to student pop-up discussions gives rich formative data about vocabulary gaps and next mini-lessons.
quotes: The non-freaked out (NFO) framework for literacy instruction across the content areas (see Fig. 1) is my attempt to create a manageable list of instructional habits that, as we work through our course content and curricula, can be used to focus our efforts.

In my own instruction, I use the framework to make both on-the-fly and planned instructional decisions. If, at the end of the year, my students are better 1) thinkers, 2) readers, 3) writers, 4) speakers, and 5) people as a result of my ninth grade world history and English courses, then I feel that I have done my job.

Content knowledge matters. Kids need to know stuff; they need to know how one comes to know stuff.[1] So, do not think of this framework as a substitute for solid, content-rich curricula in social studies and science and career/technical subjects and English language arts; do think of it as a simple, focused pathway for working through that curricula in a richer, stronger manner.[2]

The kind of argument I’m talking about is beautiful. It is deep, critical, collaborative cognition. I pray all my students – and all humans, really — become adept at it because it makes us better people.

Does argument, then, not sound awfully similar to critical thinking? Yet to me, it’s a superior word, namely because critical thinking has suffered a death-by-linguistic-extension (AKA buzzwordification) similar to close reading.[5]

One of the benefits of the NFO framework is that it gives me five sandboxes within which to play as a teacher-learner. There are a million directions in which we can expend our energies as teachers, but that is a hopeless pursuit if our aim is to maximize the positive impact of our careers.
